segments.narration: A phospholipid has a water-friendly head and two water-avoiding tails. In water, these molecules arrange themselves into two layers with their tails protected between them. This bilayer forms spontaneously because shielding the tails allows surrounding water molecules to adopt a more favorable, disordered arrangement.

The membrane is not a rigid sheet: lipids move rapidly within their own layer, while movement between layers is rare without protein assistance. The fluid mosaic model also places proteins within this moving lipid sheet. Unsaturated tails have kinks that prevent tight packing and help maintain fluidity.

segments.goal: Compare facilitated diffusion with active transport
segments.narration: Channels and carriers help substances cross the membrane down their concentration gradients without direct energy input. Carrier transport can reach a maximum rate when all carriers are occupied. Moving against a gradient requires energy; the sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move sodium out and potassium in.

Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane toward the solution with more dissolved particles. Osmolarity counts those particles rather than focusing on their identity. For example, sodium chloride produces roughly twice as many particles per formula unit as glucose does.

segments.goal: Compare hypotonic and isotonic effects on cells
segments.narration: In a hypotonic solution, water enters cells: an animal cell may swell and burst, while a plant cell becomes firm. In an isotonic solution, there is no net water movement. The animal cell keeps its normal volume, but the plant cell becomes limp.

segments.goal: Relate hypertonicity and penetrating solutes to cell volume
segments.narration: A hypertonic solution draws water out, shrinking an animal cell and pulling a plant cell's membrane away from its wall. Equal initial particle concentrations do not always prevent swelling. Urea can enter a red blood cell, and water follows, causing the cell to swell.

An ideal osmometer model predicts volume changes by assuming trapped solute stays inside while water moves until concentrations match. If the outside concentration is half the initial inside concentration, the model predicts that cell volume doubles. Real cells contain solids, however, so this is only an approximation.

Cells contain charged molecules that draw in ions and water, creating a tendency to swell. The sodium-potassium pump helps counteract this tendency. Cells can also respond to changes in volume: swollen cells release solutes so water follows, while shrunken cells can take up ions.
To recap, water moves across a membrane by osmosis. In plant cells, that movement affects turgor pressure and how firm the cells feel.
